title: How LLMs Distort Our Written Language
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how large language models (LLMs) change human writing, with a focus on whether AI writing assistance merely improves wording or instead alters meaning, stance, voice, and evaluative judgments. The authors study this question across three contexts: a randomized human writing experiment, a counterfactual comparison of human versus LLM revisions to the same essays, and an observational analysis of AI-generated scientific peer reviews. The broader concern is that widespread use of LLMs for writing may homogenize language and distort intended meaning in education and institutions.

The main intervention studied is LLM-assisted writing and revision. In the human experiment, 100 Prolific participants were randomly assigned either to write an argumentative essay without AI or with access to an embedded LLM (gpt-4o-mini). The authors further distinguished between participants who used the LLM minimally and those who relied on it heavily. In a second analysis, they used the ArgRewrite-v2 dataset of 86 essays written by university students in 2021 and compared the human revised drafts with counterfactual revisions generated by three LLMs (gpt-5-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, claude-haiku) under several revision prompts, including grammar-only and minimal edits. They also examined ICLR 2026 peer reviews to compare human-written and LLM-generated reviews in a professional setting.

The populations and contexts are not secondary-school students. The human experiment involved adult Prolific participants in the United States, and the revision dataset involved 86 university students writing argumentative essays. The writing tasks were conducted in an online research environment rather than a classroom intervention. The paper does not study ChatGPT-generated feedback on high-school student-authored drafts, and it does not report subgroup analyses by baseline writing proficiency, English learner status, disability, grade level, gender, school achievement level, subject area, or writing genre within grades 9-12. It also does not report follow-up or delayed posttests on unaided writing after feedback removal, independent revision skill transfer, self-efficacy, metacognition, plagiarism, or overreliance in a secondary-school educational design.

The main conclusions are that heavy LLM use makes essays less creative and less reflective of the writer’s own voice, while also shifting argumentative stance toward neutrality. In the essay-revision analyses, LLMs made much larger semantic, lexical, grammatical, and emotional changes than human revisers, even when instructed to make only grammar corrections or minimal edits. Across settings, the authors conclude that current LLMs systematically steer writing toward a common semantic style, often changing conclusions and reducing personal voice, with implications for education, authorship, and institutional decision-making.
quality_tier_rationale: The paper includes an RCT-like user study and quantitative analyses, but it is not a K-12 secondary education study, the main writing sample is adults/university students, and it is currently an arXiv preprint with limited education-specific relevance for the requested population. For the target KG use case, this yields only partial credibility/relevance alignment.
impact_tier_rationale: For writing-related outcomes, the reported impacts are primarily adverse: heavy LLM use reduced perceived voice/creativity and increased neutralized argumentative stance. Because the requested focus is secondary students receiving ChatGPT feedback on drafts, and this paper provides no positive delayed-transfer evidence in that population, the practical impact tier is best coded as negative/no beneficial impact.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based writing assistance and revision of argumentative essays, including co-writing, grammar editing, minimal edits, completion, and expansion of student-authored drafts; also analyzes effects on authorial voice and semantic meaning.
LLMs are prompted to revise essays using expert human-written feedback, functioning as automated draft-feedback/revision tools applied to existing student essays.
Embedded conversational LLM (gpt-4o-mini) is available for naturalistic back-and-forth support during essay writing, including idea generation, advice, and text generation.

finding.finding_summary: Across a randomized human writing study (N=100) and a counterfactual revision analysis of 86 argumentative essays, heavy LLM use and LLM-based revision altered argumentative stance, semantics, vocabulary, and syntactic style in ways that diverged from human-authored writing. In the user study, extensive AI use increased neutral responses to the essay prompt by 68.9% relative to the human condition (reported p=0.017/<0.036), and in the revision analyses LLMs made substantially larger semantic and lexical changes than humans even under 'grammar-only' or minimal-edit instructions; standardized effect sizes were not reported.
finding.measure: Argumentative stance classification, semantic embedding shift (PCA/t-SNE), lexical divergence (JSD), part-of-speech distributions, LIWC analytic language, qualitative examples of meaning/voice change in essays
finding.study_size: n=100 user study; n=86 essays in ArgRewrite-v2
finding.effect_size: 68.9% increase in neutral essays for heavy LLM users; other effect sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Heavy LLM users reported that their essays were significantly less creative and less in their own voice than participants writing without LLMs, despite similar satisfaction and similar perceived writing struggle. Reported tests showed lower creativity ratings (t(69)=2.110, p=0.0385) and much lower 'essay in my voice' ratings (t(69)=5.799, p<0.001) for heavy LLM users; no subgroup analyses for secondary students were provided.
finding.measure: Post-study Likert self-reports on creativity, satisfaction, writing struggle, organization difficulty, and whether the essay felt in the writer's voice
finding.study_size: n=100 overall; comparison reported with df=69 for heavy-LLM vs control analyses

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents evidence that LLM-assisted writing undermines preservation of authorial voice and may displace independent judgment by shifting writers toward common semantic and argumentative patterns. Heavy LLM use produced more neutral argumentative stance and more analytic/statistical language, while the paper did not report delayed unaided writing, transfer, independent revision skill, or metacognitive follow-up outcomes.
finding.measure: Authorial voice self-report, semantic clustering of essays, LLM-as-a-judge argument type categories, qualitative analysis of stance and meaning distortion
finding.study_size: n=100 user study; n=86 essays in revision analysis

finding.finding_summary: Outside education specifically, the paper finds that AI-generated peer reviews in a large scientific conference dataset differed systematically from human reviews, assigning scores about 10% higher on average (4.43 vs 4.13) and shifting evaluative criteria away from clarity/relevance and toward reproducibility/scalability. This institutional analysis used 18k reviews from 9k papers and reported highly significant z-tests for multiple category differences, but it is not a grades 9-12 education sample.
finding.measure: Peer-review scores, LLM-as-a-judge coding of strengths/weaknesses, proportions of review categories, z-tests comparing human vs LLM-generated reviews
finding.effect_size: Average score difference 4.43 vs 4.13 (~10% higher for LLM reviews); category shifts such as +136% reproducibility mentions and -32% clarity strength mentions
